name: Forecast
intent: Write down a dated, falsifiable prediction now, so it can be scored honestly later.
when: styles with a return (Ritual, Series, or a Sitting that schedules one); the duration variant also resolves within a single Sitting

variants.label: Estimate how long each of today's tasks will take
variants.prompt: Before each task, fill one circle per 30 minutes you expect it to take. Write the start time, then the actual time when it's done.
variants.readback: Compare the filled circles against the actual time for each task, the same day. An empty start or actual column means the estimate was skipped, not just missed.

claims.claim: Writing down a duration estimate before a task and comparing it with the actual duration afterwards reduces later underestimation, because people otherwise misremember how long past tasks took.
claims.construct: the planning fallacy; memory bias for past durations; feedback on estimates

claims.claim: After an outcome is known, people misremember their earlier probability estimates as closer to the outcome than they were. A dated, written prediction removes that memory distortion when the forecast is scored.
claims.construct: hindsight bias (the memory-design "I knew it" effect)

claims.claim: Making explicit probability forecasts and then receiving outcome feedback or scores improves calibration over successive rounds.
claims.construct: calibration training; forecasting with scoring rules

claims.claim: Breaking a task into its ordered component steps before predicting when it will be done reduces optimistic bias in completion-time predictions.

grounding.helps: when a day's tasks can be estimated before starting and timed as they finish; people underestimate durations partly because they misremember how long past tasks took, but the evidence that seeing actual durations improves later estimates is mixed, and it seems to help most when the next task is like the last
grounding.backfires: when the actual times go unrecorded, so the next estimate leans on a memory that runs short, or when past overruns are explained away as one-offs, which is how people keep discounting their own track record

prompt: Base rate first, then your probability, then how you'll know. Don't revise it later; score it.
readback: Record the forecast as written, then score it at the return. A few forecasts are noisy; look at the pattern over many, not at one hit or miss.

claims.claim: Making explicit probability forecasts and then receiving outcome feedback or scores improves calibration over successive rounds.
claims.construct: calibration training; forecasting with scoring rules

claims.claim: After an outcome is known, people misremember their earlier probability estimates as closer to the outcome than they were. A dated, written prediction removes that memory distortion when the forecast is scored.
claims.construct: hindsight bias (the memory-design "I knew it" effect)

claims.claim: Starting a prediction from the base rate for its reference class ("how often does this kind of thing happen?") improves forecast accuracy compared with starting from the specifics of the case.
claims.construct: the outside view / reference-class forecasting; base-rate neglect

claims.claim: A number written or seen earlier pulls later numeric judgements towards it, so a gut score written *before* criteria scoring cannot be anchored by the total.

grounding.helps: when a prediction will resolve before the next return; a dated written probability stops hindsight rewriting what you believed, a moderate and well-replicated bias, but learning calibration from a handful of scored forecasts is untested
grounding.backfires: when forecasts are judged by how they turned out rather than by the probability given, a robust bias that affects even people who say outcomes should not count, when too few forecasts are scored to learn from, or when the base-rate line is written and then ignored as not applying to this case
